St. Basil the Great

St. Basil of Caesarea · Basil the Hierarch

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

2Corinthians13:14

John 14:16–17

King James Version · Scripture previews

The selected fifteenth-century Novgorod icon of Basil is held by Norway’s National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design. It is a full-length historic hierarch portrait.

What is depicted

Basil wears a cross-patterned episcopal omophorion and holds a book. The narrow panel preserves the whole figure. These are visible attributes of this selected work; the profile does not infer a specific liturgical action from his pose.

[1] Exact file record File:Novgorod School - Saint Basil the Great - NG.M.01523 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg,field title; Exact file record File:Novgorod School - Saint Basil the Great - NG.M.01523 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.DateTimeOriginal; Exact file record File:Novgorod School - Saint Basil the Great - NG.M.01523 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Artist; Exact file record File:Novgorod School - Saint Basil the Great - NG.M.01523 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.Credit; Exact file record File:Novgorod School - Saint Basil the Great - NG.M.01523 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg,field imageinfo.extmetadata.LicenseShortName

History and tradition

Wace’s historical dictionary identifies Basil as bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and connects his family with Macrina, St. Gregory of Nyssa, and Peter. Its biography is an authored historical assessment; Basil’s own words are supplied separately below.

[2] Wace1911,entry Basilius,bp.of Caesarea in Cappadocia,opening biography/family paragraph

Published explanation

Through the Holy Spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascension into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of sons, our liberty to call God our Father, our being made partakers of the grace of Christ, our being called children of light, our sharing in eternal glory, and, in a word, our being brought into a state of all "fulness of blessing," both in this world and in the world to come, of all the good gifts that are in store for us, by promise hereof, through faith, beholding the reflection of their grace as though they were already present, we await the full enjoyment.

A verified historical English translation of Basil’s own work, distinct from the image’s later painter and date.

[3] On the Holy Spirit, chapterXV, section36; Blomfield Jackson’s 1895 translation
